title: Why synchronizing on String literal / interned object is a bug: use private final Object lock
shortTitle: Why is synchronizing on a String literal a bug?
keyPoints: String literals are interned: the JVM stores one instance per unique literal in the String pool, shared across the entire JVM.
Two unrelated classes synchronizing on the same string literal lock on the same object, causing unexpected blocking.
The same problem applies to Boolean.TRUE, Boolean.FALSE, and Integer values in the cached range (-128 to 127).
The fix is private final Object lock = new Object(): private (no external access), final (no reassignment), unique (not shared).
synchronized(this) is also risky because external code holding a reference to your object can lock on it.
SonarQube and IntelliJ flag synchronization on interned objects as a critical bug.

s1_definition.oneliner: String literals are interned and shared across the entire JVM, so synchronizing on a String literal accidentally creates a global lock that blocks unrelated code.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **String interning** – the JVM maintains a String pool with one instance per unique literal. `"LOCK"` in Class A and `"LOCK"` in Class B are the exact same object in memory.
- **Accidental global lock** – if two unrelated classes synchronize on `"LOCK"`, they lock on the same object. One class's critical section blocks the other, even though they have no relationship.
- **Cached objects** – `Boolean.TRUE`, `Boolean.FALSE`, and `Integer.valueOf(n)` for n in the range -128 to 127 are also shared singleton instances. Synchronizing on them has the same problem.
- **Fix** – always use `private final Object lock = new Object()`. Private: no external code can access it. Final: it cannot be reassigned. `new Object()`: unique to your class, not shared with anyone.
s1_definition.analogy: Synchronizing on a String literal is like using the front door key of the building as your vault key. Every shop in the building has the same front door key. When you lock your vault with this key, you accidentally lock the entire building. Two shops trying to lock at the same time deadlock each other. The fix is to give each shop its own unique key that nobody else possesses.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  String Pool (JVM-wide):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  "ACCOUNT_LOCK" ──▶ Object@0x7f3a    │
  │  "REPORT_LOCK"  ──▶ Object@0x7f3b    │
  │  "LOCK"         ──▶ Object@0x7f3c    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  AccountService: synchronized("ACCOUNT_LOCK") ──▶ locks Object@0x7f3a
  ReportService:  synchronized("ACCOUNT_LOCK") ──▶ locks Object@0x7f3a (SAME!)
  Both classes block each other!

  Fix: private final Object lock = new Object();
  AccountService.lock ──▶ Object@0xaaaa (unique)
  ReportService.lock  ──▶ Object@0xbbbb (unique)
  Different objects: no blocking!
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Synchronizing on a String literal is a bug because String literals are interned: the JVM stores one instance per unique literal in the String pool, shared across the entire JVM. If two unrelated classes synchronize on `"LOCK"`, they lock on the exact same object, causing unexpected blocking and potential deadlock between code that has no relationship.

The same problem applies to `Boolean.TRUE`, `Boolean.FALSE`, and cached `Integer` values in the range -128 to 127. All are shared singleton instances.

The fix is always `private final Object lock = new Object()`. Private prevents external access. Final prevents reassignment. `new Object()` creates a unique instance. This three-word pattern is the correct foundation for every lock in your code.

Remember one sentence: never synchronize on interned objects like String literals or cached Integers; always use a private final Object as the lock.
